title: Uplift Academy Ohio
summary: Free STEM learning, volunteer mentorship, and a summer 2026 showcase of 70+ student innovation ideas.
need: I wanted younger students to explore coding, engineering, and technology without cost determining whether they could participate. I also wanted those opportunities to continue beyond a single event.
initiative: Through the Ohio division of Uplift Academy, I developed NextGen Coders and NextGen Mentors and organized a summer innovation camp centered on the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. The camp connected hands-on STEM activities with sustainability and global challenges.
contribution: I led program development, volunteer coordination, partnerships, and planning. Keeping activities free required coordination with community organizations and the people contributing their time.
people: Students, families, volunteers, MidPointe Library, and Mason Public Library helped make the camp possible. Supplied program photographs appear in the case study without participant names.
results: Summer 2026 program-reported results: 3,500+ student learning hours, 850+ volunteer service hours, 200+ showcase attendees, and 70+ innovation ideas representing all 17 SDGs. The inaugural NextGen Coders cohort at Mason Public Library (January 6–March 17, 2026) reported 600+ student learning hours, 450+ volunteer service hours, 30 learners, and 60+ showcase attendees.
reflection: At the showcase, students explained ideas they had spent time developing. Seeing other people listen to them made the planning feel worthwhile. The experience taught me to ask whether a program works for the children, families, volunteers, and partners involved.
next: Uplift Sparks was developed for children receiving motor therapy. Expansion into Title I schools and underserved communities is described as a goal, not a completed expansion. Current delivery status needs confirmation.

title: Mason Venture Studio
role: Founding partner & Director of Programs & Operations
summary: Helping student founders move from an idea to practical experience, with mentors beside them.
need: An ambitious idea does not always come with a clear starting point. Students needed a place to try business and nonprofit ideas, find guidance, and learn through the process of building.
initiative: I helped establish a school-based, yearlong entrepreneurship program at Mason High School. It connects business ideation, market research, product development, business planning, and pitch preparation.
contribution: My work included program structure, operations, student recruitment, strategic planning, and coordinating relationships with entrepreneurs and industry mentors. I also represented the program to visiting schools and educational leaders.
people: The work belongs to student founders, mentors, educators, and the wider program team. My role was to help create the conditions and connections for their ventures to develop.
results: The initial program involved 12 startup teams. Four advanced to competition and one qualified for national competition, according to the brag sheet. The competition names, reporting period, and official results require confirmation.
reflection: Sometimes a student needed a next step; sometimes they needed expertise I did not have. I learned that listening and connecting someone with the right mentor could be more useful than supplying an answer myself.
next: The source describes presentations to the Mason City Schools Board of Education and opportunities associated with the OSBA Capital Conference. Exact dates and event materials are being confirmed before adding a dated speaking record.

title: MindMate Health
summary: Exploring how technology can make mental wellness resources easier to reach.
need: I began with a question about access: even when resources exist, reaching them can be difficult. That question led me to explore a digital wellness platform.
initiative: The project brings together emotional check-ins, journaling, personalized wellness tools, and resources. The source also describes dashboards intended for therapists and educational institutions. These are descriptions of development work, not independently verified product capabilities.
contribution: I worked on product development, technical architecture, user experience, business strategy, and outreach. Learning often began with a specific design or technical problem I needed to solve.
people: Conversations with mental health professionals helped me examine assumptions and think beyond whether a feature worked technically. The source describes exploring pilots and testing, not confirmed clinical validation.
results: I developed a platform and presented the venture through Junior Achievement competitions. Precise competition rankings need reconciliation; there is no verified user count or evidence of clinical effectiveness in the supplied material.
reflection: Setbacks made me more willing to revise an approach. Professional feedback helped me ask whether I understood the problem accurately and whether a feature belonged in the solution.
next: Current deployment, pilot status, and product claims need confirmation. This is a founder’s project account, not a treatment recommendation or a claim of proven health outcomes.

title: ME Experiential Learning
summary: Connecting elementary learning with high-school mentorship and practical financial education.
need: Third- and fourth-grade students could benefit from opportunities to explore financial literacy, entrepreneurship, and practical problem solving.
initiative: The source describes bringing Junior Achievement curriculum into elementary classrooms and connecting younger learners with high-school volunteers.
contribution: I developed the mentorship model, recruited and selected volunteers, and managed curriculum implementation, planning, and coordination.
people: Elementary students, high-school mentors, and educational partners participated at different stages of the learning process.
results: The source documents the program model and activities but does not supply a verified participant total, exact dates, or an evaluation of learning outcomes.
reflection: The initiative connects two kinds of opportunity: younger students can explore unfamiliar ideas, while older students practice teaching and leadership.
next: Confirm delivery dates, partner documentation, and participation records before adding numerical results.

title: ATMIYA Hybrid Stock Market Program
summary: Making financial concepts tangible through teaching, research, and simulated portfolios.
need: Financial concepts can be difficult to understand without an opportunity to apply them. I wanted students to explore how markets and investment decisions work.
initiative: I developed a curriculum covering financial markets, fundamental and technical analysis, portfolio management, and risk. Sessions used simulated trading accounts rather than real investment capital.
contribution: I taught approximately two to three sessions per month, explained concepts, answered questions, and encouraged independent research.
people: The source describes approximately 60 students worldwide participating in the education initiative.
results: Approximately 60 participants and $100,000 of virtual capital per simulated account are self-reported. The virtual balance is a teaching tool, not assets managed, funding raised, or an investment return.
reflection: Teaching required me to understand the reasoning behind a concept well enough to explain it. It connected my interest in finance with helping someone else learn.
next: Confirm the program period and enrollment records before adding a dated impact report.

title: The Journal of Interdisciplinary Inquiry
summary: Creating a structure for students to practice research, review, and scholarly communication.
need: Student researchers need opportunities to develop their writing and learn how scholarly review works across disciplines.
initiative: I established a student-led journal with research sections spanning medicine, mathematics, engineering, AI, law, ethics, and public policy.
contribution: I developed the organizational structure, submission guidelines, editorial procedures, and a peer-review process, and coordinated student editors and academic advisors.
people: Student authors, editors, and advisors form the intended research community.
results: The source documents organizational work; it does not establish a verified issue count, indexed status, acceptance rate, or readership.
reflection: Building an editorial process made research quality and scholarly integrity practical responsibilities.
